nameStory: The purple marsh crab gets its name from the beautiful purple-tinged coloration that often decorates its shell, especially along the edges and joints. This handsome crab is perfectly matched to its marshy home, where it scuttles among the salt-tolerant grasses and muddy channels of coastal wetlands.
description: The purple marsh crab is a small, sturdy crab that calls New England's salt marshes home. These compact crabs typically measure about 1-2 inches across their square-ish shell, with a brownish or olive-green base color often highlighted by striking purple markings. They have the classic crab body plan with ten legs total - eight walking legs plus two claws - and small, dark eyes that peek out from their flat carapace. You'll spot them scurrying sideways across mudflats or ducking into burrows when disturbed.

idTips.label: Purple coloration
idTips.description: Look for distinctive purple or violet tinges along the shell edges, leg joints, and claw tips - this purple accent against the brownish shell is like the crab's signature color scheme

idTips.label: Square shell shape
idTips.description: The carapace feels smooth and hard, roughly square-shaped rather than round, about as wide as it is long when viewed from above

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Small enough to fit comfortably in your palm at 1-2 inches across, with a stocky, robust build that feels substantial despite their small size

idTips.label: Claw size
idTips.description: Both claws are roughly the same size and relatively small compared to the body, not dramatically oversized like some crab species

idTips.label: Burrow behavior
idTips.description: Often seen darting into small, round holes in the mud - their burrows are typically pencil-width and smell distinctly of salt marsh muck

habitat: Purple marsh crabs thrive in the salt marshes along New England's coast, especially in the muddy areas between high and low tide lines. You'll find them in the soft, squishy mud among salt marsh grasses like cordgrass, often near tidal creeks and channels where the brackish water regularly floods and drains. They prefer the middle to upper marsh zones where the mud stays moist but isn't constantly underwater.

seasonality.spring: Crabs become more active as waters warm, emerging from winter burrows and beginning to molt their shells. Look for freshly shed shells along the marsh edges.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when crabs are most visible scuttling across mudflats during low tide. This is the best season for observation as they're actively feeding and most colorful.
seasonality.fall: Crabs remain active through early fall, preparing for winter by feeding heavily. Their purple coloration may be most vibrant during this time.
seasonality.winter: Crabs retreat deep into their burrows and become largely inactive. Surface activity is minimal, though they may occasionally emerge during warmer spells.

funFact: Purple marsh crabs are incredible ecosystem engineers - a single crab can move up to 15 pounds of mud per year while digging and maintaining its burrow system, essentially redesigning the marsh landscape grain by grain!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with fiddler crabs, but purple marsh crabs have two similarly-sized claws while male fiddler crabs have one dramatically oversized claw. Remember: purple marsh crabs are "fair fighters" with matched claws, while fiddler crabs look like they're carrying a boxing glove.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "purple" marsh crabs, the purple coloration can sometimes be quite subtle or absent in younger individuals, so don't expect every crab to look deeply purple. The name comes from the tendency for mature crabs to develop these distinctive purple highlights, especially during breeding season.
compareHints: As the only Sesarma species commonly found in New England, purple marsh crabs are most easily confused with other small marsh crabs in different families. Unlike green crabs which are larger and more aggressive, or fiddler crabs with their unequal claws, purple marsh crabs maintain their distinctive square-ish shell shape and balanced claw size. Their purple accents and preference for the upper marsh zones also set them apart from most other regional crab species.
